newsitem.title: HUNGARY: FIAT TOPPLES VW IN C.EUROPE IN FEB.
newsitem.headline: FIAT TOPPLES VW IN C.EUROPE IN FEB.

text.p: Fiat SPA beat back Volkswagen AG to regain the sales lead in central Europe's booming market for new autos in February, according to a monthly Reuters survey.
Fiat outsold VW 19,682 units to 17,409 units in the countries comprising the Central European Free Trade Agreement (CEFTA) -- the Czech Republic, Hungary, Poland, Slovakia and Slovenia.
South Korean conglomerate Daewoo Group
remained the region's clear third power, but its challenge for the lead started to stall. The company sold 11,512 units in February 1997, compared with 11,598 units the previous month.
No other automaker sold over 6,000 units in February.
Trailing the Big Three of central Europe were U.S. automaker General Motors Corp selling 5,602 units and French automaker Renault SA selling 5,577 units.
"Fiat and VW are rapidly raising their manufacturing capacity in central Europe to world-class standards," Philip Wade, a partner in British auto consultancy Harbour Wade Brown, told Reuters.
"Each has different things going for them, and I expect them to continue to compete closely for the lead," Wade added.
Fiat -- including Alfa Romeo, Fiat, Iveco, Lancia and several specialty brands -- led VW in CEFTA sales from the time the trade pact was created in 1993 until 1995.
The German automotive group -- including Audi, SEAT, Skoda and VW brands -- overtook the Italian conglomerate in 1996 and kept a narrow lead in January 1997.
The data, based on information that Reuters obtained from a variety of sources, include cars, minibuses, pickups, vans and other four-wheeled motor vehicles not over five tonnes in gross weight.
Overall, the market continued to slow from its all-time peak in 1996, when sales rose 39.5 percent to 842,577 units.
Sales increased only 19.4 percent to 77,229 units in February 1997 from 64,663 units in Februay 1996. Year-on-year sales grew 19.7 percent in January 1997.

But CEFTA still looked dynamic compared to western Europe, where year-on-year sales fell 1.3 percent in February 1997, according to the European Automobile Manufacturers Association, known by its French acronym ACEA.
Though Fiat recaptured the lead, some analysts said that VW remained the region's strongest player.

"VW has the best range of brands to cover these markets," British auto analyst Maxwell Pemberton told Reuters. "Skoda already is well known in the region, and it is now recognised for quality because of its affiliation with VW."
VW has continued to centre its CEFTA strategy upon Czech brand Skoda, but it also plans to assemble models from each of its brands throughout central Europe.
The German automotive group assembles SEATs and Skodas in Poland as well as VWs in Poland and Slovakia. By mid-1998, it plans to start assembling Audis in Hungary.
Fiat has focused more narrowly on CEFTA. It owns the region's biggest car factory, located in Poland, but it builds no vehicles elsewhere in central Europe.
The Italian conglomerate sells twice as many brands as VW in CEFTA. But some of Fiat's brands, such as Ferrari and Maserati, feature only high-priced specialty cars that sell in low volumes.
As a result, Fiats accounted for 98.1 percent of the Italian group's sales in central Europe in February, while Skodas represented only 58.9 percent of VW's sales.
Daewoo, which plans to build more than 500,000 vehicles a year in central Europe by 2000, has boosted its sales mainly by buying state-owned automakers in the Czech Republic and Poland.

Most analysts doubt Daewoo can sell the entire output in the region, but the South Korean conglomerate said it plans to export significant volumes throughout former communist Europe, and some units already have been shipped to western Europe.
